power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Early biomarkers of durable response to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) are urgently needed.

We identify lymphocyte stability (LS) -preservation of peripheral lymphocyte counts after one cycle of ICB -as an on-treatment predictor of overall survival (OS) in metastatic melanoma (MM): patients with unstable lymphocyte counts (LS-U; post-ICB/baseline ≤0.8) have markedly increased risk of death.

Metabolic profiling of patient T cells demonstrates ICB enhancement of mitochondrial bioenergetics, whilst CD8+ T cells from LS-U patients mount an exaggerated transcriptional response to ICB incorporating upregulation of mitochondrial pathways.

Given these findings we assessed the relationship of LS with mitochondrial haplogroup, revealing carriage of haplogroup T (HG-T), present in ~10% of white British individuals, is associated with both LS-U and impaired OS, with mediation analysis implicating LS mediation.

HG-T carriers have higher CD8+ T-cell pre-treatment mitochondrially encoded transcript abundance and, in paired scRNAseq data, fewer progenitor-exhausted cells, ICB hyperresponsivity, apoptotic program induction and reduced clonal persistence -consistent with baseline mitochondrial priming.
These findings position LS as a clinically accessible marker of ICB outcome linked to inherited mitochondrial variation.

Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), consisting of monoclonal antibodies that target the checkpoint proteins PD-1, CTLA-4 and LAG-3, forms the mainstay of treatment for patients with advanced unresectable or metastatic melanoma (MM) and is increasingly central to the management of many other cancers.

Marked heterogeneity between patients in terms of clinical benefit from ICB is apparent however, with over half of patients treated with combination anti-PD-1 (nivolumab) and anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) for MM having disease-specific survival at 10 years, the rest progressing and dying within five years 1 .

text.text: A comprehensive understanding of the determinants of variation in response to ICB promises to advance treatment stratification and development and is of major clinical and immunological interest.

Although early efforts to explain this heterogeneity focused on tumour features that confer sensitivity or resistance to ICB, it is increasingly clear that patient systemic immunity is cardinal to anti-tumour activity.
One such factor is the ability to mount a robust lymphopoietic response after ICB initiation.

This was originally described in early clinical trials of ipilimumab for MM, where patients who maintained peripheral blood lymphocyte counts (LC) after two cycles of treatment had a reduced risk of death 2 .

text.text: We hypothesise that the lymphopoietic response to ICB represents effective re-invigoration of T-cell function, linked to T-cell clonal expansion and antigen recognition, together with parameters of overall immune fitness, including sufficient lymphotropic cytokines.
In keeping with this, human genetic studies implicate IL-7, a cytokine central to lymphogenesis and peripheral T-cell homeostasis 7 , in mediating the lymphopoietic response to ICB.

text.text: After replicating our original observation of impaired OS in patients with MM with a post-ICB LC ≤0.8 baseline (lymphocyte-unstable, LS-U), we defined the core transcriptional determinants of LS in CD8+ T cells.

Patients with post-ICB LC >0.8 baseline LC (lymphocyte-stable, LS-S) displayed transcriptional induction of IL-7 signalling and mitochondrial biogenesis, whereas those with LS-U demonstrated pronounced induction of pathways linked to oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial activity.
text.formatted: Patients with post-ICB LC >0.8 baseline LC (lymphocyte-stable, LS-S) displayed transcriptional induction of IL-7 signalling and mitochondrial biogenesis, whereas those with LS-U demonstrated pronounced induction of pathways linked to oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial activity.

text.text: Functional analysis of patient-derived primary T cells pre-and post-ICB demonstrates pervasive enhancement of T-cell metabolic parameters by ICB, consistent with the crucial role of T-cell mitochondria in ICB response.
We reasoned that if mitochondrial function contributes causally to LS, a relationship between germline mitochondrial variation and LS may exist.
To test this, mitochondrial haplogroups were imputed across patients from germline genotyping.

This revealed a striking association between LS and carriage of mitochondrial haplogroup T (HG-T), which encodes non-synonymous HG-specific Complex I variants and is carried by approximately 10% of the white British population 20 .

text.text: HG-T carriers are more likely to be LS-U and have reduced OS, with mediation analysis supporting a causal relationship between HG-T effect on LS and association with OS.
Consistent with the haplogroup genetic divergence, HG-T carriers have altered expression of a discrete subset of mitochondrial encoded genes core to respiratory complexes.
Single-cell RNA-seq analysis of CD8+ T cells further linked HG-T to reduced proportions of progenitor exhausted cells.
Our findings demonstrate that LS forms a robust and easily discernible on-treatment predictive biomarker of survival post-ICB in MM, and HG-T carriage is one determinant of impaired LS.
This work underlines the dependence of durable response to ICB on systemic immune fitness, and highlights T-cell mitochondrial function as a promising therapeutic target in cancer immunotherapy.

text.text: Given the relationship between ICB and induced expression of mitochondrial pathway related transcripts, the functional metabolic correlates of treatment with ICB were explored.
To date, the effect of ICB in primary patient T cells on mitochondrial activity has not been functionally assessed.

We therefore used the Seahorse XF Tcell Persistence Assay to perform comparative paired analysis of patient sourced T cells pre and post ICB, using negatively selected T cells from patient PBMCs (n=35 paired samples).

T-cell oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) were measured, with sequential addition of drugs perturbing mitochondrial electron transport chain function (Oligomycin, BAM15 and rotenone with antimycin A respectively) and bioenergetic profiles assessed throughout (Figure 3A, Table S6).

text.text: Together, ICB not only elevates overall energy demand but also enhances metabolic flexibility, enabling T cells to dynamically engage both oxidative and glycolytic pathways in response to stress.

Coupled with the distinct hypermetabolic CD8+ T cell state observed in LS-U patients following ICB, these findings implicated mitochondrial function as a potential determinant of variation in lymphocyte stability and ICB outcomes.

Motivated by the enrichment of mitochondrial metabolic pathways in LS-associated genes, we investigated the potential role for variation in innate mitochondrial characteristics to modulate the interaction between LS and ICB efficacy.

text.text: Given that LS-U was associated with both HG-T carriage and shorter OS, we next asked whether the adverse clinical impact of HG-T is mediated through its effect on LS.
To address this, we performed causal mediation analysis, modelling LS status by logistic regression, HG-T as the exposure and OS by a Weibull accelerated failure time (AFT) model.
Both models were adjusted for age, sex, CMV serostatus, cancer type, and ICB regimen.
In the full cohort, HG-T carriage was associated with shorter OS (time ratio [TR] 0.43, 95% CI 0.21-0.88, P = 0.021; n = 370).

Among patients with available LS data (n = 294), in whom the mediation analysis was performed, the effect of HG-T on OS was of similar magnitude, albeit with borderline significance (TR 0.50, 95% CI 0.24-1.04, P = 0.063).
Within this subset, HG-T carriers had approximately four-fold higher odds of LS-U (OR 4.08, 95% CI 1.80-9.22, P = 6.6×10 -4 ).
In turn, LS-U was independently associated with shorter OS (TR 0.35, 95% CI 0.20-0.61, P = 1.9×10 -4 ).
After LS status was included in the survival model, the association between HG-T and OS was attenuated and no longer significant (TR 0.65, 95% CI 0.31-1.37, P = 0.26).
Causal mediation analysis identified a significant indirect effect of HG-T on OS acting through LS.

This effect corresponded to an average reduction of approximately 22 months in model-predicted survival time (average causal mediation effect [ACME] -21.7 months, 95% CI -47.0 to -5.5, P = 0.004), whereas the direct effect of HG-T was not significant (average direct effect [ADE] -38.2 months, 95% CI -97.7 to 39.1, P = 0.25) (Figure 4G).

text.text: Treatment selection in MM however is based on clinical and tumour-intrinsic factors, and does not take account host T-cell fitness.
Clinically, preemptive identification of ICB non-responders is attractive for its potential to identify non-responding patients early so as to enable treatment switching and escalation.

Here we show that LS -lymphocyte stability -representing the ratio of lymphocytes derived from routine blood tests across the first cycle of ICB, identifies patients with impaired long-term survival in MM well in advance of standard radiological assessment timepoints.
We further show that LS reflects underlying divergent CD8+ T-cell mitochondrial activity, with an exaggerated oxidative transcriptional response to treatment characterising poorer outcomes.

Notably, LS is in part determined by inherited mitochondrial variation: carriage of mitochondrial haplogroup T (HG-T) being associated with ICB hyperresponsiveness, reduced progenitor-exhausted TPEX compartment, impaired T-cell clonal persistence and shortened OS.
Lymphocyte stability (LS), the preservation of peripheral lymphocyte counts after one cycle of ICB, is a dynamic on-treatment indicator of OS across anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4 regimens.

After adjustment for clinical covariates, LS remains prognostic and further stratifies patients with elevated baseline NLR, suggesting that it captures on-treatment prognostic information distinct from baseline indices.

Paired CD8+ T cell RNA-seq pre-and post-ICB revealed a substantially greater response in LS-U patients (more DEGs, larger effects), preferentially involving oxidative phosphorylation and electron transport chain pathways.

Conversely, LS-Sassociated pathways were characteristically anabolic, including positive regulation of mitochondrial translation and IL-7 signalling, consistent with preserved biosynthesis and homeostatic survival.

In addition, although PD-1 signalling regulates T-cell glycolysis, fatty-acid oxidation and oxidative activity 44 , the bioenergetic effects of checkpoint blockade in patient T cells remain incompletely characterised 45 .

text.text: We propose a priming-activation-attrition model to integrate these observations.

For HG-T, inherited mitochondrial variation establishes a primed baseline state, upon which ICB imposes increased bioenergetic demand; the greater induction of respiratory-chain programmes in HG-T cells may therefore reflect increased demand or compensatory adaptation rather than greater mitochondrial fitness.
Baseline CD8.
TPEX depletion with reduced MYB-associated programmes is consistent with this state being one of increased cellular stress.

After ICB, increased apoptotic programmes and reduced clonotype persistence suggest that altered metabolic adaptation in HG-T favours activation and differentiation at the expense of progenitor maintenance and clonal persistence.

Our study thus identifies LS as an integrative on-treatment phenotype, linking clinical outcome with T-cell metabolism and clonal persistence during ICB, derivable from routine blood testing and therefore potentially scalable for dynamic monitoring during therapy.
The association of HG-T with lymphocyte instability provides evidence that inherited mitochondrial variation can shape T-cell capacity to meet the metabolic demands of ICB.

Metabolic adaptability, rather than activation alone, is a potential determinant of sustained immunity -which may help explain why strong effector activation does not necessarily translate into durable response.

As inhibition of additional checkpoints has yielded limited improvement beyond PD-1-based therapy 53 , our findings build on recent work that suggests approaches to support Tcell mitochondrial function 54 , rather than further releasing inhibitory brakes, may represent a complementary strategy to enhance ICB.

text.text: First, the study remains predominantly observational.
HG-T is present in only a subset of LS-U patients, indicating that it represents one inherited contributor rather than a deterministic cause of lymphocyte instability.
Other host-, tumour-, and treatment-related factors likely contribute to LS.
Second, although our transcriptional and cellular findings are consistent with altered mitochondrial adaptation in HG-T CD8+ T cells, they do not directly establish mitochondrial dysfunction.
Seahorse experiments assessed ex vivo stimulated T cells, rather than tumour-reactive CD8+ T cells, and were underpowered for HG-T-specific phenotypes.
Further functional comparisons are required to distinguish compensatory adaptation and intrinsic respiratory dysfunction.
Finally, short-read sequencing cannot completely resolve . homologous mtDNA and NUMT sequences.
Although our variant-aware alignment substantially reduced genotype-dependent read misassignment, residual ambiguous mapping is likely to remain.
Long-read sequencing, ideally incorporating haplotyperesolved mitochondrial and nuclear genomes, will be important for validating haplogroup-associated mitochondrial transcription.

text.text: Peripheral blood samples (30-50 mL) were collected prior to initiation of immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) and longitudinally before each subsequent treatment cycle.
Plasma and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated by Ficoll-Paque density gradient centrifugation.

PBMCs were processed as follows: (i) cells were lysed in RLT Plus buffer (Qiagen) supplemented with dithiothreitol (DTT; Merck) and snap-frozen at -80 °C for RNA and DNA extraction; (ii) immune cell subsets were enriched using magnetic-activated cell sorting (MACS) (Miltenyi Biotec) for downstream bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing; and (iii) aliquots were cryopreserved in 90% fetal calf serum (FCS; Gibco) with 10% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO; Merck) for future use.
Peripheral blood plasma collected at baseline (day 0) was diluted 1:2 in HBSS and used to quantify CMV IgG titres on an Abbott Architect i2000 immunoassay platform.
For all analyses, the blood sample obtained closest to treatment initiation (within -30 to 0 days) was used as the baseline time point.
Patient demographic and clinical characteristics were extracted from the electronic patient record (EPR).

Disease stage was assigned according to American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition staging system, with Tumour Node Metastasis (TNM) 8th edition criteria for metastasis subclassification (M1a-d).
All patients included had a minimum follow-up duration of 6 months for survival analyses.
PFS was defined as time of ICB initiation to clinical or radiological evidence of progression (according to irRECIST.1.1 criteria), or death.
OS was defined as time from ICB initiation to death from any cause.
Median follow-up duration was determined using a reverse Kaplan-Meier method.

To calculate lymphocyte stability (LS) and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), full blood counts were obtained from EPR, where they were generated via Sysmex XN series analyzers (Sysmex Corporation) in an NHS clinical diagnostic laboratory.

Pretreatment (C1) samples were defined as the most recent sample prior to ICB initiation (from Day -30 to Day 0), and post-treatment (C2) samples were the most recent sample after the first treatment cycle (from Day 18 to Day 50).
Patients with a prior diagnosis of lymphoid-lineage haematological malignancies (e.g. chronic lymphocytic leukemia, lymphoma) were excluded.

text.text: The optimal cutpoint for LS at 0.8 was determined by maximally selected log-rank statistics using surv_cutpoint() function from survminer (version 0.5.1).
This was supported by time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis using pROC (version 1.19.0.1), where the 24-month optimal cutoff was 0.804 based on maximal Youden index.

Poly(A)-selected RNA libraries were sequenced using either 150-bp paired-end reads on an Illumina NovaSeq platform or 75-bp paired-end reads on an Illumina HiSeq 4000, both performed at the Oxford Genome Centre.
Sequencing reads were aligned to the GRCh38/hg38 reference genome using HISAT2 (version 2.2.1), and gene-level read counts were generated with HTSeq (version 2.0.9).
High-quality alignments were retained based on mapping quality (MAPQ) scores using bamtools (version 2.

To account for sequence-dependent misalignment between mitochondrial transcripts and nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs), we generated a mitochondrial variant-aware alignment reference based on GRCh38.

Mitochondrial variants associated with the haplogroups represented in the cohort, together with conservative mitochondrial variants (AF ≥ 0.01) catalogued in the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) v3.1, were incorporated into the HISAT2 reference as SNP and haplotype information, while retaining the complete nuclear genome to permit competitive alignment between mitochondrial and homologous nuclear loci.

HISAT2 indices were generated using hisat2-build with the --snp and --haplotype options, and paired-end RNA-seq reads were subsequently realigned to the resulting variant-aware reference using HISAT2.
Gene-level expression was re-quantified from the variant-aware alignments using HTSeq-count with the same annotation and counting parameters applied to the original analysis.
These re-derived counts were used for all downstream analyses involving mitochondrial and nuclear mitochondrial pseudogene expression.
TPM values were calculated from the re-quantified gene counts using gene lengths derived from the corresponding GRCh38 annotation.
Genes with low expression were filtered prior to analysis, retaining only those with a mean count > 10 across samples.

text.text: For longitudinal comparisons between baseline (C1) and post-treatment cycle 2 (C2) samples, DE analysis was conducted in a paired manner using the subset of 174 matched samples, incorporating patient identity as a blocking factor in the design formula to account for inter-individual variability.

For cross-sectional comparisons between HG-T and Non-T groups at each time point (baseline and post-treatment), the top three principal components derived from variance-stabilised expression data were included as covariates in the design matrix, unless otherwise specified, to mitigate potential technical variation.
We performed GSEA using fgsea (version 3.22) with MSigDB Gene Ontology Biological Process (GOBP) datasets.
Genes were ranked by average log₂ fold change (FC) derived from DE analysis.
To ensure comparability between contrasts, only overlapping genes between the two groups were retained as the background set.

To minimise selection bias and enhance robustness, enriched pathways were ranked based on the difference in normalised enrichment scores (ΔNES) between groups, and the top-ranked pathways were selected for visualisation.

Overrepresentation analysis was conducted using clusterprofiler (version 4.18.4) with MSigDB GOBP gene sets with DEGs from each comparison tested against the shared gene universe using a hypergeometric test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing.
Enriched pathways were ranked by fold enrichment, and the highest ranking terms were visualised.
Mitochondrial complex-specific gene sets were curated from MSigDB (C2:CP:WikiPathways; complexes I-IV) and the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (HGNC; complex V).
Normalised gene expression values were extracted from baseline and post-treatment samples, and pathway activity scores were calculated as the geometric mean of gene expression within each complex.

To assess the interaction between mitochondrial haplogroup status and treatment over time, linear mixed-effects models were fitted using patient ID as a random effect to account for repeated measurements.
Fixed effects included mitochondrial haplogroup, treatment time point, and their interaction term.
T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire profiling was performed on bulk CD8+ RNA-seq data from paired pre-and post-treatment samples using MiXCR (version 3.0.13).
Sequencing reads were aligned to reference V, D, and J gene segments to reconstruct TCR clonotypes based on complementarity-determining region 3 (CDR3) sequences.
To improve clonotype assembly, the non-default parameter OallowPartialAlignments = true was enabled to retain partially aligned reads for downstream assembly.
Three iterative rounds of partial read assembly (assemblePartial) were conducted to maximise recovery of CDR3-containing sequences.
In addition, quality-aware error correction during clonotype assembly and clustering was applied using a threshold of ObadQualityThreshold = 15.
Samples with fewer than 500 detected TCR clones were excluded to ensure sufficient repertoire complexity, and one outlier C2 sample from patient ID 250 was removed from downstream analysis.

Following quality control, a total of 431,709 TRA chains and 714,627 TRB chains were identified across 173 donors with paired samples, including 106 donors with C1/C2 pairs and 67 donors with C1/C2/C4 longitudinal sampling.
Clonotypes were defined based on the amino acid sequence of the CDR3 region in combination with TRB V and J gene usage.
Clone size was quantified using TRB chains, with clonal expansion measured as the proportion of total repertoire occupancy (clone read count / total TRB read count).
Persistent clones were defined as clonotypes present in both pre-treatment (C1) and posttreatment (C2) samples from the same individual.
Lost clones were defined as clonotypes present at C1 but absent at C2, whereas new clones were defined as clonotypes absent at C1 but detected at C2.

Positively selected CD8⁺ T cells, together with peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), were quantified and partitioned into nanoliter-scale droplets using the 10X Genomics Chromium platform, followed by cell lysis and reverse transcription.
Complementary DNA (cDNA) was used to generate 5′ gene expression (GEX) and V(D)J libraries using the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 5′ Reagent Kit v2 (Dual Index).
Droplet encapsulation and reverse transcription were performed on individual samples, whereas library preparation and sequencing were conducted in batches.
Sequencing was performed on an Illumina HiSeq 4000 platform, generating 75-bp paired-end reads for 5′ gene expression libraries and 150-bp paired-end reads for V(D)J libraries.
Raw base call (BCL) files were converted to FASTQ format using Illumina software.
Single-cell RNA-seq reads were aligned to the GRCh38 human reference genome and quantified using Cell Ranger (version 8.0.1, 10X Genomics).

To improve cell barcode recovery, droplets were additionally processed using the EmptyDrops algorithm implemented in the DropletUtils package (version 1.28.0), retaining both Cell Ranger-and EmptyDrops-identified cells.

For sample demultiplexing, bi-allelic single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were quantified at the single-cell level using cellsnp-lite (version 1.2.0), and donor identities were inferred using Vireo (version 0.5.8).
Putative heterotypic doublets were identified using scDblFinder (version 1.22.0), while additional genotypic doublets were detected via Vireo.
Ambient RNA contamination was corrected using SoupX (version 1.6.2).
Genes detected in fewer than 10 cells were excluded from downstream analyses.
Cell-level quality control criteria included (i) a mitochondrial transcript fraction <20% and (ii) detection of >300 genes per cell.
text.formatted: Cell-level quality control criteria included (i) a mitochondrial transcript fraction <20% and (ii) detection of >300 genes per cell.

text.text: Doublets identified by either scDblFinder or Vireo were removed prior to clustering and annotation.

Following preprocessing and initial annotation, 220,060 high-quality CD8+ T cells were selected from 195 samples across 120 donors (12 HG-T and 108 Non-T individuals), in which 150 samples were paired across pre-and post-treatment timepoints.
Downstream analyses were performed using Scanpy (version 1.11.5), including log-normalisation and identification of top 3,000 highly variable genes (HVGs) within the CD8+ T population.
To determine the optimal integration strategy, we benchmarked five widely used methods -BBKNN, Harmony, Scanorama, ComBat, and scVI -using the scIB-metrics framework (version 0.5.7).
Based on batch correction scores and overall performance, scVI (version 1.1.5) was selected for batch correction, modelling each experimental pool as a batch covariate.
Dimensionality reduction and clustering were performed using the scVI latent space, followed by nested Leiden clustering and visualisation using UMAP.
For automated cell type annotation, scANVI (version 1.1.5) and CellTypist (version 1.7.1) were applied for cross-dataset label transfer using external references derived from Azimuth and COMBAT.
In addition, the expression of canonical marker genes was also visualised to refine CD8+ T-cell cluster annotations.
Differential gene expression analysis was performed using Seurat (version 5.4.0) with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test implemented in the FindMarkers() function, unless otherwise specified.
For longitudinal comparisons, only pre-and post-treatment paired samples with more than 20 cells per subset were included in the analysis to ensure sufficient statistical power and representation.

To control for differences in statistical power arising from unequal cell numbers across groups, we implemented a subsampling strategy whereby each group was downsampled to the size of the smallest group (n = 1,200 cells).
This procedure was repeated 100 times, and results were aggregated to mitigate sampling variability and reduce bias.
As an orthogonal validation, DE was additionally assessed using a donor-aware linear mixed-effects model.
Genes with non-zero variance in the subsampled dataset were included, and donor identity was modelled as a random effect to account for inter-individual variability.
For post-versus pre-treatment comparisons, six donors per group were randomly selected to ensure balanced representation across conditions.
Pathway enrichment analysis was performed using clusterProfiler (version 4.18.4) with GOBP gene sets.
Up-and down-regulated genes were analysed separately using a hypergeometric test, with the background defined as all detected genes.

To compare pathway-level responses to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) between HG-T and Non-T individuals across cell subsets, enrichment analyses were conducted on each subsampled dataset (n = 1,200 cells per group).
Pathway-level differences were quantified as the delta frequency of enriched pathways between HG-T and Non-T groups across bootstrap iterations.
This approach was adopted to maximise statistical power for pathway detection, particularly in subsets with limited DE signals.
TCR chains were filtered based on productive rearrangements and chain identity (TRA or TRB).
Cells were retained if they contained either (i) a single TCRβ chain, (ii) one TCRα paired with one TCRβ chain, or (iii) two TCRα chains paired with one TCRβ chain.
Cells not meeting these criteria were excluded from downstream analyses.
In addition, samples with fewer than 100 cells containing detectable TCR clonotypes were removed to ensure sufficient repertoire coverage.
Clonotypes were defined based on the concatenated amino acid sequences of CDR3 regions present within each cell, with cells sharing identical CDR3 compositions assigned to the same clonotype.
Clonal proportions were calculated as the number of cells belonging to each clonotype divided by the total number of cells per sample that passed the above filtering criteria.
In total, 165,040 cells from pre-and post-treatment paired samples across 75 patients had matched transcriptomic data.
After quality control, 112,897 cells from 72 individuals retained high-confidence V(D)J sequencing information with valid chain configurations and were included in all downstream clonal analyses.
For analyses of clonal phenotype, cells were grouped by clonotype, individual, and time point.
The distribution of each clone across transcriptional subsets was quantified as the proportion of its constituent cells assigned to each subset.
The subset with the highest proportion was designated as the dominant phenotype of the clone.
Definitions of persistent, new and lost clones were applied as described in the MiXCR-based bulk TCR repertoire analysis section.
Single-cell gene set activity was quantified using UCell (version 2.14.0), a rankbased scoring method robust to differences in sequencing depth and data sparsity.
Gene sets were obtained from the MSigDB Hallmark collection.
To ensure adequate representation, only gene sets with more than five overlapping genes detected in the dataset were retained for analysis.
UCell scores were computed at the single-cell level based on gene expression rankings.
To summarise pathway activity at the clonal level, cells were grouped by clonotype, and the median UCell score across all cells within each clone was calculated for each gene set.
Gene regulatory network analysis was performed using the pySCENIC pipeline (version 0.12.2b0).
The raw single-cell count matrix was used as input to infer transcription factor (TF)-target interactions.
Co-expression relationships between TFs and candidate target genes were first estimated using the GRNBoost2 algorithm implemented in the grn step.
TF-target pairs with importance scores >1 were retained for downstream analysis.
text.formatted: TF-target pairs with importance scores >1 were retained for downstream analysis.

text.text: Regulons were subsequently refined using the cisTarget (ctx) step, which integrates motif enrichment analysis to identify direct TF targets.

Motif annotation was performed using the motifs-v10nr_clust-nr.hgnc-m0.001-o0.0.tbl database, and genomic rankings were derived from the hg38_10kbp_up_10kbp_down_full_tx_v10_clust.genes_vs_motifs.rankings.feather reference.
Regulon activity at the single-cell level was quantified using AUCell, which computes enrichment scores based on the ranked expression of target genes.
To assess cell type specificity, regulons were ranked within each CD8+ T-cell subset based on their regulon specificity scores (RSS).
The Illumina Global Screening Array 24 version 3 (Illumina) was used for genotyping.

For sample deconvolution of pooled single-cell data, nuclear autosomal genotypes were aligned to hg37 and assessed for call frequency > 0.9, SNP missingness < 3%, Minor Allele Frequency (MAF) > 1%, and Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) P > 10-20 using GenomeStudio (version 2.0.5, Illumina) and PLINK (version 1.9b6.24); samples with call rates < 97% were removed from further analysis.
text.formatted: For sample deconvolution of pooled single-cell data, nuclear autosomal genotypes were aligned to hg37 and assessed for call frequency > 0.9, SNP missingness < 3%, Minor Allele Frequency (MAF) > 1%, and Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) P > 10-20 using GenomeStudio (version 2.0.5, Illumina) and PLINK (version 1.9b6.24); samples with call rates < 97% were removed from further analysis.

text.text: Upon initial quality control, imputation was performed using the Michigan Imputation Server with Haplotype Reference Consortium (HRC) version 1.1 Build hg19 as a reference panel, as well as Eagle (version 2.4) and Minimac4 (version 1.7.4) for phasing and imputation.
SNPs were further screened for MAF > 4%, HWE P > 10-10 and r 2 > 0.7 and lifted-over to hg38.
text.formatted: SNPs were further screened for MAF > 4%, HWE P > 10-10 and r 2 > 0.7 and lifted-over to hg38.

text.text: Prediction of mitochondrial haplogroups For mitochondrial haplogroup prediction, mtDNA sites were aligned to the revised Cambridge Reference Sequence (rCRS).
Initial QC was performed on mitochondrial variants, retaining SNPs with call rates > 90% and MAF > 0.1%.
text.formatted: Initial QC was performed on mitochondrial variants, retaining SNPs with call rates > 90% and MAF > 0.1%.

text.text: Alleles were flipped or switched as required to guarantee alignment with rCRS orientation.
With samples designated as male, mitochondrial imputation was then carried out using a GenBank mitochondrial reference panel 82 within the IMPUTE2 (version 2.3.2) chromosome X framework.
Post-imputation QC included filtering variants with an imputation INFO score > 0.7 and resolving reference/alternate allele discrepancies.
text.formatted: Post-imputation QC included filtering variants with an imputation INFO score > 0.7 and resolving reference/alternate allele discrepancies.

text.text: HaploGrep3 (version 3.2.1) was used to assign mitochondrial haplogroups based on PhyloTree build 17.2, applying a heteroplasmy level threshold of 0.9.
Paired pre-and post-treatment PBMC samples were selected by an independent investigator prior to experimentation.

The principal experimentalist remained blinded to patient cancer type, treatment regimen, lymphocyte stability and mitochondrial haplogroup status until completion of data quality control and normalisation.
Cryopreserved PBMCs were rapidly thawed in pre-warmed R10 (RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum) and rested for 4 hours at 37°C in a 5% CO2 incubator to allow metabolic recovery.
Untouched T cells were isolated from PBMCs using negative selection (Pan T cell isolation kit, Miltenyi Biotec) according to the manufacturer's protocol.

T cells were stimulated for 16 hours on anti-CD3 (10μg/ml, BioLegend) coated plates in the presence of soluble anti-CD28 (5μg/ml, BioLegend) to mimic antigen exposure and early activation-induced metabolic remodelling.
Activated T cells were resuspended in Seahorse XF RPMI medium supplemented with 10mM glucose, 1mM sodium pyruvate and 2mM L-glutamine as per manufacturer instructions (Agilent Technologies).
Seahorse cell culture microplates were pre-coated with Poly-D-lysine (10μg/ml) for 1 hour at room temperature to facilitate cell adherence.
Activated T cells were plated at 1 x 10 5 total cells per well, with the maximum feasible number of technical replicates acquired for each sample according to cell availability.
Plates were centrifuged at 200 x g for 2 minutes, and wells were visually inspected by light microscopy to confirm uniform cell seeding.

Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) measurements were measured using the Seahorse XF Pro Analyzer (Agilent Technologies) at baseline and following sequential injection of oligomycin (1.5μM), BAM15 (2.5μM) and rotenone / antimycin A (0.5μM each).
To minimize inter-plate batch effects, paired samples from the same patient were always analysed on the same plate together with a standardized inter-plate healthy donor control.
Wells failing pre-defined quality control criteria (e.g. abnormal mitochondrial stress test profiles, injection failure, poor cell adherence) were excluded.
OCR and ECAR values were normalized to 1 x 10 5 viable cells, and scaled relative to the basal respiration of the inter-plate control.
All statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.5.3).
Survival analyses were conducted using survival (version 3.8-3) and survminer (version 0.5.1), and data visualisation was performed with ggplot2 (version 4.0.1).
Unless otherwise specified, Cox proportional hazards models and logistic regression analyses were adjusted for age, sex, CMV serostatus, and treatment type (sICB versus cICB).
Initial comparisons were performed using univariate log-rank tests in the metastatic melanoma cohort and subsequently validated in a pan-cancer cohort.
Correlation analyses were performed using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.
Comparisons between paired and unpaired groups were conducted using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and Wilcoxon rank-sum test, respectively.
Odds ratios (ORs) were estimated using Fisher's exact test, and adjusted ORs were derived from generalized linear models with a binomial distribution.
To evaluate the mediating role of LSI in the relationship between HG-T and OS, mediation analysis was performed using the mediation R package (version 4.5.1).

A parametric Weibull survival model was used for the outcome model, as it provides a fully parametric framework that facilitates estimation of direct and indirect effects under time-to-event outcomes.
Linear mixed-effects models were implemented in lme4 (version 1.1-38).
All statistical tests were two-sided.
Significance levels were defined as follows: P < 0.05, P < 0.01, P < 1x10 -3 , and P < 1x10 -4 .

A total of 246 baseline cycle 1 (C1) CD8⁺ T-cell transcriptomes (25 HG-T and 221 Non-T), 195 post-treatment cycle 2 (C2) transcriptomes (22 HG-T and 173 Non-T), and 67 post-treatment cycle 4 (C4) transcriptomes (5 HG-T and 62 Non-T) were included in the analysis.
Among these, 174 donors (21 HG-T and 153 Non-T) were longitudinally paired across time points.
Gene expression counts were normalised using DESeq2 (version 1.50.2).
